source.title: Markov Chain Estimation with In-Context Learning
source.authors: Simon Lepage; Jérémie Mary; David Picard

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper studies context-based transition estimation in synthetic Markov-chain tasks and reports attention patterns it identifies as induction heads. It uses a different task and measurement setup from the original studies.
record.gate_note: The paper reports model outcomes for transition estimation and attention patterns, including comparisons across training-set size, model size, state encodings, and test-chain structure. It does not report the cited studies' results as its own.
record.test_reason: The task is new: synthetic Markov-chain next-token prediction in a small Llama-style transformer. The paper reports, qualitatively, whether an induction-head attention pattern forms across training-set size, model size and state encoding. That bears on V5 and, weakly, on V1. The study is not an original source.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is correct: next-token training suffices to learn in-context transition estimation above model-size and data-size thresholds, and permutation and orthogonal encodings aid generalization.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains transformers on synthetic Markov-chain next-token prediction and measures transition-estimation performance and attention patterns; it does not reproduce the original studies' training-time phase-change measurement.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcomes vary with hidden size and number of training transition matrices, state encoding, test number of states, and test Dirichlet parameter alpha.

fits_no_version.finding: Learned-embedding models degrade on test chains with different k or alpha, while orthogonal-embedding models track the empirical estimator.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Robustness of in-context Markov estimation to test-distribution shift depends on the state encoding.

record.problems: The task is synthetic and does not establish results for large language models or other domains. Attention-pattern evidence is qualitative and does not causally test the proposed composition mechanism. Figures provide plotted values without reported uncertainty estimates; Figure 1 describes averages over 5 runs.

untested.parts: Composition with a previous-token head; any causal or ablation test of the mechanism; attention-only models.
When heads form during training; data domains other than synthetic Markov chains.
All of V2. There is no training-time trajectory; the 'sudden transition' is across the N and d grid.

missing.what: Whether induction heads emerge after the fix of zero-vector concatenation plus added capacity in orthogonal-embedding models. The text implies it but does not state it.

record.verdict_notes: Induction-head evidence is limited to qualitative attention maps in Figure 1 and one textual remark in Section 3.2.1. The paper's 'transition phase' refers to the grid over N and d, not to training time, so it does not bear on V2 or V7.

versions.untested_parts: It reports the appearance or absence of an induction-head pattern, but does not causally test composition with an earlier previous-token head or establish the complete [A][B] … [A] → [B] copying mechanism.
No training-time trajectory tests whether heads form in a narrow early window, coincide with a gain in later-token in-context learning, or produce a bump in training loss.
The study uses a synthetic Markov-chain task; it does not test whether induction heads account for most in-context learning in large transformers.
It does not test induction behaviour across model families, independent training runs, other architectures, or modalities.

The reported dependencies concern this synthetic Markov-chain task and its tested model sizes, training matrices, state encodings, and transition distributions—not other data domains or training setups.
It does not distinguish few-shot task learning from repeated-token copying or test alternative carriers of few-shot learning.
It does not track separate sub-steps or overlapping transitions during training.

rows.subject: Transformer (learned embeddings)
rows.size_stated: Hidden size d ranges from 8 to 512; two layers and one attention head in the learned-embedding configuration
rows.operation_detail: Inspected typical attention patterns across model-size and training-matrix-size regimes.
rows.measure: Attention pattern identified by the authors as an induction head
rows.value: The induction-head pattern appears in the generalization regime.
rows.note: The paper describes typical attention patterns for the regimes; it does not give a causal test of the full head-composition mechanism.
rows.check: The model is not attention-only: it has SwiGLU MLPs and is two layers with one head. Evidence is a typical attention pattern in Figure 1, with no composition analysis. The row also bears on V5, since the pattern appears only at large N and large d.

source_check.correct: Observed for V5. Cannot determine V1: the model includes SwiGLU MLPs, and the attention-pattern observation does not test composition with an earlier previous-token head.
source_check.problem: The observed state is justified for V5 but not for the full V1 mechanism.

rows.subject: Transformer (learned embeddings)
rows.size_stated: Hidden size d ranges from 8 to 512
rows.operation_detail: Varied hidden size and the number of training transition matrices; compared validation loss with oracle loss.
rows.measure: Validation loss relative to oracle loss; training loss and attention pattern
rows.value: Low training loss but increasing validation loss, especially for large d; authors describe memorization of training transition probabilities and uniform attention over the context.
rows.uncertainty: Figure 1 reports loss averages after 10k training steps over 5 runs; error bars or other uncertainty estimates are not stated.
rows.note: The text describes this as the overfitting regime for small N.
rows.check: For V5 the dependence is shown in full: small N gives memorization and uniform attention, with no induction pattern. The state should be observed, not partial.

rows.subject: Transformer (learned embeddings)
rows.size_stated: Hidden size d ranges from 8 to 512
rows.operation_detail: Varied hidden size and the number of training transition matrices; compared training and validation losses.
rows.measure: Training and validation loss; attention pattern
rows.baseline: Oracle loss for the reported model-loss comparison
rows.value: Both losses stagnate; the authors say the model lacks capacity to memorize the training matrices or learn a generalizing algorithm. Attention is mostly uniform, with a wavy positional bias at the second layer.
rows.uncertainty: Figure 1 reports loss averages after 10k training steps over 5 runs; error bars or other uncertainty estimates are not stated.
rows.note: The text identifies this as the underfitting regime.
rows.check: At small d (up to 32) the attention is uniform with a positional bias and no induction head forms. This shows formation depends on model size, so the state should be observed.

rows.subject: Transformer (learned embeddings)
rows.size_stated: Hidden size d ranges from 8 to 512
rows.operation_detail: Compared a single training transition matrix, with and without permutation augmentation, against training with newly sampled matrices.

conditions.value: A5M, described as equivalent to a new transition matrix for each training sequence

rows.measure: Generalization performance, measured as model loss relative to oracle loss
rows.value: The permutation scheme with a single matrix achieves performance comparable to A5M.
rows.uncertainty: Figure 1 reports loss averages after 10k training steps over 5 runs; error bars or other uncertainty estimates are not stated.
rows.note: The authors attribute the improvement to permutation augmentation generating examples from k! matrices.
rows.check: This measures generalization loss only, not induction heads. It bears on V5 only through whether in-context estimation is learned under different training data.

rows.subject: Transformer (orthogonal embeddings)
rows.size_stated: Four layers and two attention heads
rows.operation_detail: Inspected whether induction heads emerged with dynamically generated random orthogonal state embeddings.

conditions.value: random orthogonal embeddings, with a zero vector concatenated to each vocabulary vector

rows.value: The authors report that induction heads no longer emerge with this approach.
rows.note: The authors hypothesize that randomly spreading token-identifying information across dimensions makes merging tokens at the first induction-head layer destructive.
rows.check: This is a training-setup dependence (V5), not evidence against V1's mechanism, so V1 is removed. The model size and steps listed belong to the later, fixed configuration; the failing configuration's size is not stated.

source_check.correct: Induction heads fail to emerge with the initial dynamically generated random orthogonal embeddings. Zero-vector concatenation and increased capacity are subsequent mitigation steps. The failing configuration's layer count, head count and training steps are not stated; four layers, two heads and 20k steps describe the later orthogonal-embedding configuration.
source_check.problem: The row assigns the failure to the subsequent zero-padded configuration and imports that configuration's architecture and training duration.

relationships.condition: Markov-chain task, varying number of training matrices, hidden size and state encoding
relationships.reason: Induction heads appear only at large N and large d (R1). Attention is uniform at small N or small d (R2, R3). Heads fail to form with plain random orthogonal embeddings (R5). Permutation augmentation changes whether in-context estimation is learned (R4).
relationships.display_finding: Induction heads appeared only with many training matrices and large hidden dimensions; smaller settings retained uniform attention, plain random orthogonal embeddings prevented head formation, and permutation augmentation changed whether in-context estimation was learned.

statements.problem: The statement describes other studies despite citing this study's R5; it omits the orthogonal-encoding result.
